# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transfemoral arterial access remains the default route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore structural interventions. However, TAVR necessitates a large-bore access, most commonly accomplished through transfemoral arterial access; however, a subset of patients, up to 5%, may exhibit insufficient iliofemoral diameters and require alternative approaches [1]. Small, tortuous, or heavily calcified iliofemoral vessels render such patients ineligible for conventional access, and they are paradoxically often higher-risk and poorer candidates for surgical or thoracic alternative access. Transcaval (caval-aortic) access emerged to address this gap.

## Concept and physiological rationale

Caval-aortic access refers to percutaneous entry into the abdominal aorta from the femoral vein through the adjoining inferior vena cava (IVC) [2]. The approach was first validated preclinically by Halabi and colleagues, who demonstrated aortic access from the vena cava for large-caliber transcatheter interventions [3]. Its apparent safety is counterintuitive but mechanistically grounded: its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole [4]. The procedure relies on transcatheter electrosurgery—delivery of continuous, alternating radiofrequency current to cut the targeted tissue, traversing through the inferior vena cava, retroperitoneal space, and ultimately reaching the abdominal aorta [5]. The principles of guidewire electrosurgery have since been formalized in dedicated reviews [6].

## Technique and procedural planning

In practice, an electrified guidewire is directed from the IVC into a snare pre-positioned in the abdominal aorta [7]. Transcaval TAVR typically requires three vascular access sites: a large-bore venous access to deliver the transcatheter heart valve, a second venous access for transvenous pacing, and an arterial access for delivery of the snare, aortography, and bailout tamponade or covered stent if necessary [8]. After crossing, the rigid guidewire is exchanged and conventional TAVR proceeds; the aorto-caval tract is then closed with a nitinol occluder. Detailed step-by-step tutorials guide both planning and complication management [9], and contemporary "best practices" and "7 pillars" frameworks have codified the technique for new operators [4][1]. Patient selection hinges on computed tomography. Early work described how to plan transcaval access using CT for large transcatheter implants [10], and a subsequent analysis defined anatomic suitability—identifying a suitable calcium-free aortic crossing target adjacent to the IVC [11].

## Outcomes in TAVR

The first human experience was reported by Greenbaum and colleagues. Between July 2013 and January 2014, 19 patients underwent TAVR via caval-aortic access; access and tract closure were successful in all 19, and TAVR was successful in 17 [2]. The pivotal prospective NHLBI investigation followed: transcaval access was successful in 99 of 100 patients; device success occurred in 98 of 99; inpatient survival was 96% and 30-day survival 92% [12]. VARC-2 life-threatening bleeding and modified major vascular complications possibly related to transcaval access were 7% and 13%, respectively [12]. One-year tract fate was reassuring: at 12 months there were no additional vascular complications, and only 1% of aortocaval fistulae were proven patent [13]. A multicentre European registry confirmed feasibility outside the United States, concluding that transcaval access proved a feasible and safe alternative for high-risk patients not suitable for transfemoral or transaxillary/subclavian access [14].

## Comparative evidence

Single-centre comparisons have suggested favourable outcomes relative to other non-femoral routes [15]. In a propensity-weighted analysis of transcaval versus transaxillary TAVR, stroke or TIA was significantly less common after transcaval access, and significantly more patients were discharged directly home after transcaval access [16]. A systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 8 studies (467 patients) reported that a total of 8 studies with 467 patients were included, and TCv-TAVR achieved a success rate of 98.5% [17]. A network meta-analysis of access routes provides further context for positioning transcaval among alternatives [18]. The latest SCAI consensus recommends that extrathoracic access (transcarotid, transcaval, transaxillary/subclavian) be preferred over intrathoracic access for TAVR, with transapical/transaortic considered when these are not feasible [19].

## Closure and dedicated devices

A persistent limitation has been off-label use of nitinol cardiac occluders. Closure using off-label nitinol occluders has been shown to be safe, but persistent aortocaval fistulae at exit from the catheterization laboratory and bleeding complications were common [20]. A purpose-built device was therefore developed: in first-in-human testing the dedicated closure device achieved complete closure in most subjects at exit from the laboratory and essentially eliminated transcaval-related bleeding, potentially enabling wider adoption [20]. Indeed, the dissemination of transcaval access and closure techniques has been hampered by the unavailability of commercially marketed devices [4]. Special situations—such as crossing through a synthetic graft—have also been described, expanding applicability [21].

## Beyond TAVR

Transcaval access is increasingly versatile. Transcaval aortic access has been used for transcatheter aortic valves, and Uflacker and colleagues reported its use for thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) in lieu of a surgical iliac conduit owing to small atherosclerotic pelvic arteries [22]. Image guidance has been refined with intravascular ultrasound to localise the optimal aorto-caval crossing site [23]. In mechanical circulatory support, transcaval access is feasible for emergency non-surgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries [24]. Contemporary case series continue to evaluate transcaval delivery of microaxial flow pumps as a means of avoiding limb ischaemia [25][26], and the technique has extended to interventional paediatric and congenital cardiology [27]. Broader application has been catalysed by recognition that the transfemoral arterial route is unfeasible in a meaningful minority of patients, prompting development of multiple alternative pathways [28]. Comparative femoral-versus-non-femoral data underscore that any non-femoral route carries incremental risk, reinforcing the importance of careful selection [29].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from a counterintuitive concept into a validated, fully percutaneous route for delivering large-bore devices to the aorta. Transcaval access has been performed in thousands of patients for TAVR and endovascular thoracic aneurysm repair and to avoid limb ischaemia in percutaneous mechanical circulatory support [4]. With dedicated closure devices, refined CT and intravascular ultrasound planning, and accumulating comparative evidence, transcaval access is now an established option in the structural heart armamentarium when transfemoral access is not possible [30].
